question: Why is storing a growing per-user map in Instance storage a denial-of-service risk in Soroban?

golden.answer: Instance storage is part of the contract-instance ledger entry and is loaded with the contract, so unbounded per-user data makes every invocation read and deserialize more bytes. Operations can eventually hit fee, resource, or ledger-entry-size limits; an over-limit write fails and the prior valid state remains, but application paths that require further growth can become unavailable—a real DoS risk, not an automatic permanent brick. Separately, the contract-data entry-size limit is a validator-voted setting that can be lowered to a small protocol floor, and stellar-core also checks entry size when it loads footprint entries: an instance entry larger than a later-lowered limit makes every invocation fail until validators raise the limit, so leave headroom. Keep Instance storage small and fixed. Put per-user/unbounded data in separate Persistent keys and shard any growing collection.
keyFacts: Unbounded Instance storage raises every invocation's cost.
Growth-dependent paths can fail at resource or entry limits.
Over-limit writes fail atomically with prior valid state preserved.
Use Persistent keys or sharding for unbounded data.
avoid: Do NOT call the first over-limit write an irreversible permanent brick.
Do NOT say Instance storage is lazily loaded like separate Persistent keys.
golden.notes:
Routes to scout_research (security corpus). Instance = whole instance entry loaded per call; verified against the storage/state-archival semantics. Trap: thinking Instance loads lazily.
Also good if the answer: This is a recognized Soroban vulnerability class (Instance-storage DoS / unbounded storage growth) in audit checklists.
Golden cites: A Soroban security checklist (e.g., Veridise) or developers.stellar.org storage guidance.
GT-46 CORRECTION 2026-07-11: distinguish rejected writes and growth-path DoS from an unsupported permanent-brick claim.
2026-11-02 read-path qualifier: stellar-core validates contract-data entry size on footprint reads as well as writes. An answer that says an instance entry left above a later-lowered contract_data_entry_size_bytes makes every call fail until the limit is raised is correct and does not fire avoid[0]. An answer that says ordinary growth makes the existing entry unreadable or the contract permanently unusable is still wrong.
